extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (and patent prosecutors/practitioners reviewing written-description requirements)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application’s specification adequately shows that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention (written description requirement) under 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA and post-AIA). Focuses on claim-by-claim analysis, support in the specification/drawings, means-plus-function limitations, and factors tied to the level of skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is an essential part of the examination process. Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the entire claim (including preamble and transitional phrase) when assessing support. Case law: In re Katz; In re Morris; Lockwood. The examiner should analyze each claim to determine if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble and transitional phrase consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble language (language before the transitional phrase) and the transitional term affect claim scope; 'comprising' is open-ended, 'consisting essentially of' is intermediate, and 'consisting of' is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret transitional terms according to case law (Genentech v. Chiron; Ex parte Davis; PPG Indus.). Absent clear specification language defining 'consisting essentially of', treat it as equivalent to 'comprising' for prior art search/102/103 purposes. If applicant asserts exclusion based on 'consisting essentially of', applicant bears burden to show additional elements would materially change basic/novel characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the entire application to see how applicant provides support for each element/step
rubrics_metrics.description: Before determining adequacy of written description, review claims and the entire specification (embodiments, figures, sequence listings) to understand how applicant provides support for claimed features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare claim scope with disclosure scope from the viewpoint of one of ordinary skill in the art. Determine the field of the invention and the level of skill/knowledge in the art. See Rasmussen; Amgen v. Chugai.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description review is conducted from the standpoint of a person of ordinary skill in the art at the filing date and should consider the field’s level of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There may be an inverse correlation between the level of skill in the art and specificity required in the disclosure—well-known information need not be detailed. See Wang Labs.; Hybritech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether disclosure shows inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must determine whether the specification informs a skilled artisan that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a factual, case-by-case inquiry; consider multiple factors (level of skill, partial structure, properties, function, method of making). See Purdue Pharma; Pfaff v. Wells; Vas-Cath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession shown by actual reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice (constructing an embodiment or performing the process that meets all claim limitations and demonstrates the invention works for its intended purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice provides strong evidence of possession. Biological materials may be shown by deposits complying with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. Case citations: Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder; Mahurkar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession shown by detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear depiction in detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas may demonstrate possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings alone may provide a written description (Vas-Cath; Wolfensperger). Generic formulae can indicate what a genus encompasses and be adequate in chemical cases (Eli Lilly). Drawings and formulae are appropriate means where visual representation fleshes out words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession shown by relevant identifying characteristics (structure, properties, function coupled with correlation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of sufficiently detailed, relevant identifying characteristics (e.g., partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics with known correlation to structure) can evidence possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For biomolecules, examples include sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length. If the art establishes a strong correlation between structure and function, function+minimal structure can suffice (Enzo Biochem; Falkner v. Inglis; Capon v. Eshhar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-only disclosure is typically insufficient for composition claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing a composition by its function alone typically will not suffice to describe the composition for written-description purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function-only disclosure may be merely a 'wish' or plan and not demonstrate possession (Eli Lilly; Fiers). Exceptions exist where a well-established structure-function correlation allows prediction of structure from function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical inventions require precise definitional disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate written description of a chemical invention requires a precise definition by structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties, not merely a plan or wish to obtain the chemical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception of chemical compounds requires the ability to define and distinguish the compound and to describe how to obtain it (Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle & Co.; Amgen v. Chugai).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) limitations require corresponding structure/materials/acts in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA 112 sixth paragraph), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts disclosed in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must consider summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings. A means-plus-function limitation is adequately described if (1) the written description adequately links particular structure/materials/acts to perform the function, or (2) it is clear that one skilled in the art would know what structure/materials/acts in the specification perform the function. See B. Braun; Aristocrat; Atmel; Biomedino. If a means-plus-function limitation is indefinite under 112(b), it also lacks adequate written description under 112(a). See In re Noll; MPEP § 2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from the specification into the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations should not be imported from the specification into the claims when construing claim scope for written description analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the weight to be given the preamble and avoid improperly limiting claims by specification-only recitations. See Bell Communications Research; Corning; Pac-Tec.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-known or conventional information need not be detailed
rubrics_metrics.description: What is conventional or well known to one of ordinary skill in the art need not be disclosed in detail in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply written description in context of the particular invention and the state of knowledge in the art (Hybritech; Capon v. Eshhar). As the field evolves, the balance between known material and new contribution evolves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species vs genus: analyze scope relative to disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment/species is analyzed as a species claim; a claim that encompasses multiple embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 806.04(e). The disclosure required varies depending on whether the claim is to a single species or to a broader genus; follow the checklist for single-species claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist for claims drawn to a single embodiment or species
rubrics_metrics.description: For each single-species claim: (A) determine whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, determine whether the invention is complete via reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas; (C) if not, determine whether the invention is set forth via distinguishing identifying characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a complete structure is disclosed, the written description requirement is satisfied for that species. If not, determine whether other identifying characteristics (function+known correlation, partial structure+characterization) are sufficient. See detailed sub-steps (1) and (2) in the guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in determining sufficiency of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider factors such as level of skill/knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (especially when coupled with known correlations), and the method of making the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use patents and printed publications to assess art maturity and what is known. In mature fields, written description issues are less likely where only methods and functions are disclosed; in emerging/unpredictable fields, more evidence of possession is required. See Eli Lilly; Capon v. Eshhar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher evidentiary requirement in emerging or unpredictable technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions in emerging or unpredictable technologies, or those characterized by factors not reasonably predictable, more evidence is required to show possession; disclosure of method+function may not be sufficient to support a product claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product-by-process claims: written description satisfied where process has actually been used to produce the product; may not be satisfied where it is unclear that the acts in the specification can be performed or that the product is produced. Partial-structure-only disclosures without further characterization may be insufficient (Fiers; Amgen).
